steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing a scalable and transferable time series prediction framework for demand forecasting. Cover why demand forecasting matters, the limits of deep learning and ensemble approaches, how our work relates to time-series foundation models, the question that drives the paper, and how the paper is organized.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Demand forecasting
- crucial for supply chain management; inventory planning, revenue; E-commerce and offline retail need accurate forecasts
- sales forecasting competitions (M competitions) over past decades; many methods for accurate, robust prediction

2. Deep learning
- popular: flexible, many time series, no handcrafted features or extra training on new products
- often worse than classical algorithms, overfitting
- hard to scale model size; we observe single large model (hundreds of layers / thousands of hidden states) performs poorly on our datasets

3. Foundation models
- recent studies: foundation models for time-series forecasting
- large-scale model, generalize to unseen data zero-shot, not instance-specific
- our work resonates with trend; pioneering scalable, transferable framework for demand forecasting

4. Ensembles
- combining classical + deep learning: relatively successful; robustness to distribution shift
- forecasting the future -> shift between training, validation, test periods inevitable
- selecting/assigning base models from pool is hard
- careless ensembling: smoothing / disharmonizing, lower accuracy
- demand forecasting: hundreds of thousands of series, each with different temporal characteristics -> worse
- conventional ensembles: user-defined set of individually trained base models
- prior work: deep ensemble improves accuracy + OOD robustness when base models explore different modes in function space

5. Question / framework
- how to construct many distinct but jointly-working base models and guide them flexibly?
- scalable, flexible time series prediction framework (Figure 1)

6. Organization
- Sec II framework and training; Sec III literature (demand forecasting, ensemble forecasting, representation learning for time series); Sec IV and V qualitative/quantitative studies on E-commerce and M5

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Demand forecasting is a crucial part of supply chain management. Both E-commerce and offline retail stores need accurate forecasts of future demand for the products they offer, so that they can make better inventory planning decisions and maximize revenue. Because of this, several sales forecasting competitions like the M competitions have been held over the past decades, and various forecasting methods have been proposed for more accurate and robust time series prediction.

Recently, deep learning-based algorithms have become popular because they are flexible, which means they can be applied to a wide range of time series without needing handcrafted features or additional training on new products. But their performance is often even worse than classical algorithms, because they tend to overfit. These methods also have trouble scaling up their model size effectively, and in this paper we also observe empirically that a single large model with hundreds of layers or thousands of hidden states performs poorly when forecasting on our datasets.

Very recently, several studies have tried to build foundation models for time-series forecasting. These foundation models try to build a large-scale forecasting model that generalizes to unseen data in a zero-shot manner, instead of building instance-specific forecasting. We believe our work fits with this growing trend, as one of the first efforts to build a scalable and transferable framework (for demand forecasting).

Ensembles
- combining classical + deep learning: relatively successful, partly due to robustness to distribution shift
- predicting the future -> shift between training, validation, test periods inevitable
- selecting/assigning base models from pool is hard
- careless ensembling: smoothing or disharmonizing results, lower accuracy
- demand forecasting: hundreds of thousands of series, different temporal characteristics each -> issues more pronounced
- conventional: user-defined set of individually trained base models
- prior work: deep ensemble improves accuracy + OOD robustness when base models explore different modes in function space

Question and framework
- how to construct many distinct but jointly-working base models and guide them more flexibly?
- scalable, flexible time series prediction framework (Figure 1)

Organization
- Section II: framework and training; Section III: literature (demand forecasting, ensemble forecasting, representation learning for time series); Sections IV and V: qualitative + quantitative studies on E-commerce and M5

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Demand forecasting is a crucial part of supply chain management. Both E-commerce and offline retail stores need accurate forecasts of future demand for the products they offer, so that they can make better inventory planning decisions and maximize revenue. Because of this, several sales forecasting competitions like the M competitions have been held over the past decades, and various forecasting methods have been proposed for more accurate and robust time series prediction.

Recently, deep learning-based algorithms have become popular because they are flexible, which means they can be applied to a wide range of time series without needing handcrafted features or additional training on new products. But their performance is often even worse than classical algorithms, because they tend to overfit. These methods also have trouble scaling up their model size effectively, and in this paper we also observe empirically that a single large model with hundreds of layers or thousands of hidden states performs poorly when forecasting on our datasets.

Very recently, several studies have tried to build foundation models for time-series forecasting. These foundation models try to build a large-scale forecasting model that generalizes to unseen data in a zero-shot manner, instead of building instance-specific forecasting. We believe our work fits with this growing trend, as one of the first efforts to build a scalable and transferable framework (for demand forecasting).

Ensemble approaches that combine classical and deep learning methods have also been relatively successful in time series forecasting. Part of the reason is that they are more robust to distribution shift. Time series prediction requires inference on the future, where no data has been observed, so a distribution shift between the training, validation, and test periods is inevitable.

Even though ensemble learning has benefits, it is still hard to select and assign base models from the pool. If ensembling methods are not applied carefully, they can end up smoothing or disharmonizing the forecasting results and lowering forecast accuracy. Also, for problems like demand forecasting, where hundreds of thousands of time series need to be forecasted, the issues are even bigger, because each time series instance has different temporal characteristics that a model has to capture and extend into the future.

Also, conventional ensemble methods often rely on a user-defined set of base models that have been trained individually. But according to prior work, an ensemble of deep learning models can improve its accuracy and out-of-distribution robustness when each base model is trained to explore different modes in the function space. So this paper is shaped by the question: How can we construct a large number of distinct but jointly-working base models and guide them in a more flexible manner? To address this question, we present a scalable and flexible time series prediction framework, shown in Figure 1.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. In Section II we describe in detail how the proposed framework works and how it is trained. Section III introduces literature in demand forecasting, ensemble forecasting, and representation learning for time series. Finally, in Section IV and Section V we present extensive qualitative and quantitative studies that analyze the proposed model in depth, using two large-scale real-world demand forecasting datasets, E-commerce and M5.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Demand forecasting is a crucial component of supply chain management: to make better inventory planning decisions and maximize revenue, both E-commerce and offline retail stores require accurate forecasts of future demand for the products they offer [1]. Accordingly, several sales forecasting competitions, such as the M competitions [2,3,4,5,6], have been held over the past decades, and various forecasting methods have been presented for more accurate and robust time series prediction.

Deep learning-based algorithms have recently gained popularity due to their flexibility, which allows them to be applied to a wide range of time series without requiring handcrafted features or additional training on new products [6]. However, their performance is often even worse than that of classical algorithms due to their tendency to overfit [7,8]. These methods also struggle to scale up their model size effectively, and in this paper we empirically observe that a single large model with hundreds of layers or thousands of hidden states performs poorly when forecasting on our datasets.

Very recently, several studies have attempted to build foundation models [9] for time-series forecasting [10,11,12]. Rather than building instance-specific forecasting, these foundation models aim to build a large-scale forecasting model that generalizes to unseen data in a zero-shot manner. The authors believe this work resonates with this burgeoning trend, as one of the pioneering endeavors to conceive a scalable and transferable framework (for demand forecasting).

Meanwhile, ensemble approaches combining classical and deep learning methods have seen relatively high success in the time series forecasting domain, partly owing to their increased robustness to distribution shift; since time series prediction requires inference on a future where no data has been observed, a distribution shift between the training, validation, and test periods is inevitable [13].

Despite the benefits of ensemble learning, selecting and assigning base models from the pool remains challenging [14]. If ensembling methods are not applied carefully, they risk smoothing or disharmonizing the forecasting results and lowering forecast accuracy. Moreover, for problems like demand forecasting, where the number of time series to be forecasted is in the hundreds of thousands, these issues become even more pronounced, because each time series instance has different temporal characteristics that a model needs to capture and extend into the future.

In addition, conventional ensemble methods often rely on a user-defined set of individually trained base models. According to [15], however, an ensemble of deep learning models can improve its accuracy and out-of-distribution robustness when each base model is trained to explore different modes in the function space. This paper is therefore shaped by the question: How can we construct a large number of distinct but jointly-working base models and guide them in a more flexible manner? To address this question, we present a scalable and flexible time series prediction framework, illustrated in Figure 1.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we describe in detail how the proposed framework works and is trained. Section III introduces literature in demand forecasting, ensemble forecasting, and representation learning for time series. Finally, in Section IV and Section V, we present extensive qualitative and quantitative studies analyzing the proposed model in depth on two large-scale real-world demand forecasting datasets, E-commerce and M5.
